Federal and state law enforcement agencies arrested more than 230 undocumented immigrants, including more than 40 commercial driver’s license holders, during a 72-hour enforcement operation spanning 15 states.
The operation, dubbed Operation Guardian , was conducted Oct. 26-28 by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and state and local law enforcement partners, according to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
It targeted immigrants DHS described as holding unauthorized CDLs, along with other individuals the agency identified as public safety threats connected to the trucking industry.
Operation Guardian follows recent truck blitzes in Arkansas , Arizona, California, Kentucky and North Dakota .
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin announced the results Monday during a news conference at Melton Truck Lines’ headquarters in Tulsa, Oklahoma.
The operation involved authorities in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Iowa, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Tennessee and Texas.
DHS did not provide a state-by-state breakdown of Operation Guardian arrests or identify which states accounted for the more than 40 CDL holders detained.
The announcement also did not specify which states issued the licenses, the number of commercial vehicles inspected or how many CDL holders were actively operating trucks when apprehended.
Operation Guardian follows another federal immigration enforcement initiative targeting commercial vehicles.
On Sept. 25, ICE launched Operation Guardrail, a nationwide effort targeting commercial vehicles operating in violation of U.S. laws.
As of Oct. 29, ICE had arrested 303 people through Operation Guardrail, according to DHS.
The agency also reported that between Jan. 20, 2025, and Oct. 28, 2026, ICE made 4,795 CDL-related arrests nationwide, including 1,233 arrests involving CDL holders.
However, DHS did not explain whether the latest Operation Guardian arrests were included in its cumulative figures or whether any individuals arrested were charged with licensing fraud or other CDL-related offenses.
The agency also did not release information establishing how many of the detained CDL holders had obtained their licenses through fraudulent applications or were otherwise ineligible to hold them.
Why it matters: The coordinated crackdown signals escalating federal and state scrutiny of commercial drivers’ immigration status and CDL eligibility.

The Chinese surprised the HPC community earlier this year when they took the top spot on the TOP500 list with LineShine, an all-CPU machine out of the National Supercomputing Center in Shenzhen that recorded 2.2 exaflops on the Linpack test. With the launch earlier this year of the long-delayed Sugon 8000 supercluster in Zhengzhou, the Chinese now have publicly acknowledged four exascale-class machines.
The Sugon 8000, also known as “Dengfeng,” is a 100,000-card supercluster developed by Sugon Information Industry Co. , one of the country’s leading developers of supercomputers and AI clusters. The system is located at the National Supercomputing Center in Zhengzhou (also known as the Henan Supercomputing Center), and is hooked into the country’s National Supercomputing Internet.
We don’t know a lot about the technical particulars of this system, which has been delayed for years. But we know a few things. For starters, it’s based on chips made by Hygon Information Technology , a developer of X86-compatible CPUs and AI accelerators, among others. It uses Sugon’s new interconnect, dubbed scaleFabric, the “InfiniBand-like” 400G/800G RDMA network that it introduced earlier this year.
Storage for the Sugon 8000 is provided by ParaStor, the flash-based parallel file system developed by Sugon for HPC and AI training. Sugon recently submitted the ParaStore for global IO500 list, where it took first place full-node and 10-node rankings. (Glenn Lockwood recently described the ParaStor F9000 as “very WEKA-like” in his blog ).
The Sugon 8000 is composed of 10,000 computing cards (Image courtesy Sugon)
Dengfeng uses Sugon’s proprietary “immersion phase-change liquid cooling” in support of “single-cabinet MW-class high power-density deployment,” according to Sugon’s July announcement . The new system is an example of China’s “HPC-AI fusion” technology, the company says. Sugon says that Dengfeng will support a range of workloads, from scientific codes requiring full FP64 all the way to running AI models in INT8 mode.
Sugon says the new system is significant because it represents an expansion beyond 1,000-card and 10,000-card cluster to 100,000-card clusters: “The official completion of Sugon 8000 (Dengfeng) offers a reference sample for 100,000-card AI infrastructure and shifts evaluation of large computing-power centers from scale stacking and performance contests toward more comprehensive system capability, with greater weight on real application efficiency and industrial economic productivity,” the company says.
Sugon says the new supercluster has already been used for 300 different applications, ranging from large AI models and drug discovery to astronomy and quantum computing. The company says 70 applications have been validated on the expansion from 10,000-card clusters, apparently paving the way for new “scientific intelligence” workloads to come to the cluster, including protein-folding simulation, trillion-atom-scale water molecular dynamics, and ultra-large-scale turbulence simulation, along with large AI models and agentic AI.
There are a lot things we don’t know about the new system. For instance, we don’t know how many processors it has, what sorts of accelerators (if any) it uses, what type of memory it uses, and how much. We don’t know how many racks the cluster is composed of, nor do we know about its specific power requirements.
We also don’t know if the Sugon 8000 will be listed on the TOP500 list when the latest edition comes out later this month at SC26. After LineShine took first place at ISC 2026 in June, it’s possible that the Chinese are more willing to share their HPC creations with the world. Unless there is a surprise announcement (which is always possible), it seems unlikely that new leadership-class American systems will debut at the top of the list when Jack Dongarra, Horst Simon, Erich Strohmaier, and Christine Harvey debut the new list on Tuesday, November 17, at SC26 in Chicago, Illinois.
China’s exascale ambitions are no secret. LineShine may be the first and only Chinese system to officially break the exaflop barrier with a published Linpack score, but with the introduction of Sugon 8000, the country now is believed to have at least four exascale machines (and maybe more). The other two that we know about include the Sunway Oceanlite cluster built by the National Supercomputing Center in Wuxi, and Tianhe-3 installed at the National Supercomputing Center in Guangzhou.
Former HPCwire Editor Tiffany Trader provided a detailed account of Oceanlite and Tianhe-3 systems in this November 2021 story . As Trader wrote five years ago, the new Sugon cluster based on X86-compatible CPUs–as well as a Hygon DCU (“like a GPU”)–had been delayed for years. That system was initially planned to use the Hygon Dhyana CPUs, which is an x86 architecture derived from AMD ‘s 2016 joint venture with THATIC.
However, following the 2019 sanctions the US Government placed on THATIC and Sugon, the Chinese decided to forge ahead with their own chip development program without assistance from AMD. That’s one of the big reasons for the multi-year delay.
